title: Pompeii's Last Day: What Really Happened in AD 79
alt_titles: The Pompeii Date Historians Can't Agree On
Pompeii: A Roman Town Frozen in Time
description_summary: In AD 79, Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum in less than two days. Using Pliny the Younger's eyewitness letters and the latest archaeology, this is what we know about the town's final hours, and why even the date of the eruption is still debated.

scenes.narration: In AD 79, at the Roman naval base of Misenum on the Bay of Naples, a young man called Pliny was at his studies. Early one afternoon, his mother pointed out a cloud of unusual size and shape rising across the water. It came from a mountain on the far side of the bay, called Vesuvius. Within two days, the towns at its foot had vanished, and thousands of lives had changed for ever.

shots.caption: An eruption of Vesuvius, by Pierre-Jacques Volaire, 18th century

scenes.narration: That cloud marked the start of one of the most famous disasters in history. It buried Pompeii and its neighbours so completely that they lay hidden for more than fifteen hundred years. When they were finally found, they revealed something almost no other place could: a Roman town caught in the middle of ordinary life.

shots.caption: The Last Day of Pompeii, by Karl Bryullov, painted 1827 to 1833

shots.caption: The Forum of Pompeii with Vesuvius behind, painted by Christen Købke

scenes.narration: But the story we tell about Pompeii's last day is less certain than it looks. Even the date is argued over. So this video follows the evidence. We will look at what the people of Pompeii left behind, what one eyewitness wrote down, and what archaeologists are still discovering today.

shots.caption: Plaster casts of victims, 19th-century photograph

scenes.narration: Pompeii stood on the southern side of the Bay of Naples, a few miles from Vesuvius. Its first clearly recognisable phases date to the late seventh and sixth centuries BC, shaped by local Italic peoples, Etruscans and Greeks. Under the Samnites, between the fourth and second centuries BC, it grew into a prosperous town.

shots.file: File:Map around Vesuvius 1770 plate6 from William Hamilton.jpg
shots.query: map Bay of Naples Vesuvius 18th century
shots.caption: Map of the area around Vesuvius, published 1770s

shots.query: Pompeii Samnite house Casa del Fauno atrium
shots.caption: A Samnite-era house in Pompeii

scenes.narration: In 89 BC, during Rome's Social War, Roman forces besieged the town. Afterwards the general Sulla established a Roman colony there, in 80 BC. Its official name became Colonia Cornelia Veneria Pompeianorum, and the town became firmly part of the Roman world.

shots.caption: Portrait bust traditionally identified as Sulla
Pompeii's city walls and gate

scenes.narration: By the first century AD, Pompeii was a busy place of shops, bakeries, bars, temples and grand houses. Exactly how many people lived there is not known. Modern estimates range from around ten thousand to twenty thousand, and historians still debate the figure.

shots.file: File:Sommer, Giorgio (1834-1914) - n. 1237 - Pompei - Casa di Cornelio Ruffo.jpg
shots.caption: The House of Cornelius Rufus, photographed by Giorgio Sommer
A bakery with millstones in Pompeii

scenes.narration: We can even see some of their faces. A wall painting from one house shows a married couple, usually identified as the baker Terentius Neo and his wife. She holds a writing tablet and a stylus, and he holds a scroll. Both look straight out at us. It is one of the most personal images to survive from the Roman world.

shots.file: File:Fresco from Pompeii - Terentius Neo and his wife 1.jpg
shots.query: Terentius Neo and his wife fresco
shots.caption: Portrait of a Pompeian couple, fresco, 1st century AD

shots.file: File:Fresco portrait of the baker Terentius Neo and his wife, from Pompeii.jpg
shots.caption: The couple usually identified as Terentius Neo and his wife

scenes.narration: The ground here was not always kind. In AD 62, a severe earthquake struck the area. It damaged houses, temples and public buildings, and rebuilding went on for years afterwards. To the people living around the bay, Vesuvius itself was simply a mountain of vineyards and farmland.

shots.query: Pompeii earthquake relief lararium Caecilius Iucundus
shots.caption: A relief from Pompeii thought to show the earthquake of AD 62

shots.query: Bacchus and Vesuvius fresco House of the Centenary
shots.caption: Wall painting of Bacchus beside a vine-covered mountain

scenes.narration: Then the mountain erupted. Pliny the Younger later described the cloud as looking like a pine tree. It rose on a tall trunk and spread out into branches at the top. Volcanologists still call this kind of explosive eruption Plinian, after him.

shots.file: File:Pierre-Henri de Valenciennes Eruption du Vesuve Musée des Augustins Toulouse 78 1 1.jpg
shots.caption: The eruption of AD 79 imagined by Pierre-Henri de Valenciennes, 1813

shots.file: File:Pierre-Jacques Volaire - View of the Eruption of Mount Vesuvius - WGA25290.jpg
shots.caption: An eruption column over Vesuvius, painted by Volaire

scenes.narration: Out of that column, pumice and ash began to rain down across the countryside, including Pompeii. The lightweight stones piled up in the streets, in courtyards and on roofs. Over the following hours, the town disappeared beneath several metres of volcanic debris.

shots.file: File:Karl Brullov - The Last Day of Pompeii - Google Art Project detail3.jpg
shots.caption: Detail from The Last Day of Pompeii, Karl Bryullov
A street in Pompeii after excavation

scenes.narration: Many people seem to have left in these first hours. Others stayed, sheltering indoors or trying to gather their belongings. We will probably never know how many got away, or where they went.

shots.file: File:Karl Brullov - The Last Day of Pompeii - Google Art Project detail1.jpg
shots.query: Last Day of Pompeii detail fleeing
shots.caption: Fleeing families, detail from Bryullov's painting
The Via dell'Abbondanza, one of Pompeii's main streets

scenes.narration: Most of what we know about these hours comes from two letters. More than two decades after the disaster, Pliny the Younger wrote to his friend, the historian Tacitus. He described what he had seen himself, and what had happened to his uncle.

shots.query: Pliny the Younger statue Como cathedral
shots.caption: Statue of Pliny the Younger on Como Cathedral
Statue of the historian Tacitus

scenes.narration: His uncle was Pliny the Elder, the author of a vast encyclopedia called the Natural History. In AD 79 he commanded the Roman fleet at Misenum. When he saw the strange cloud, he ordered a ship to be prepared so that he could take a closer look.

shots.file: File:Caius Plinius Secundus. Stipple engraving by F. W. Bollinger Wellcome V0004719.jpg
shots.caption: Pliny the Elder, imagined in a later engraving

shots.file: File:Pliny the Elder, Natural History, Florence, Plut. 82.4.jpg
shots.caption: A medieval manuscript of Pliny the Elder's Natural History

scenes.narration: According to his nephew, a message then arrived from a woman named Rectina. Her villa lay at the foot of the mountain, and the only way out was by sea. What had begun as scientific curiosity became a rescue mission. He launched warships and sailed straight towards the danger, while others were fleeing from it.

shots.caption: A Roman warship, from an ancient relief

shots.file: File:Pierre-Jacques Antoine Volaire - Eruption of Mount Vesuvius with the ponte della Maddalena in the Distance.jpg
shots.query: Volaire eruption Vesuvius Ponte della Maddalena
shots.caption: Vesuvius erupting over the bay, painted by Volaire

scenes.narration: He reached Stabiae, where his friend Pomponianus was staying, and tried to calm everyone there. The letter says he bathed, dined and even slept, while outside the ash and stones kept building up.

shots.caption: A fresco from a Roman villa at Stabiae

shots.file: File:Eruption of Vesuvius - Pierre-Jacques Volaire (40288534610).jpg
shots.caption: The eruption at night, painted by Volaire

scenes.narration: Eventually they had to make for the shore, with pillows tied to their heads against the falling stones. There, Pliny the Elder collapsed. His nephew believed thick fumes had choked him. When his body was found, it was unhurt, and he looked as if he were asleep.

shots.query: death of Pliny the Elder engraving Stabiae
shots.caption: The death of Pliny the Elder, as imagined by a later artist
The coast at Stabiae, looking towards Vesuvius

scenes.narration: In a second letter, Pliny described his own escape. The next morning, as the ground shook, he and his mother left Misenum with crowds of frightened people. A dark cloud came down over the bay. He wrote that the darkness was deeper than any night, and that people called out for their families in the gloom.

shots.query: Pliny the Younger letter Vesuvius engraving darkness
shots.caption: Pliny's escape from Misenum, as imagined by a later artist

shots.query: Misenum Capo Miseno Bay of Naples
shots.caption: Cape Misenum, where the Roman fleet was based

scenes.narration: The deadliest phase came later. As the eruption changed, its column collapsed into pyroclastic currents. These were avalanches of scorching gas, ash and rock that raced down the mountain's slopes and across the land below.

shots.file: File:Karl Brullov - The Last Day of Pompeii - Google Art Project detail4.jpg
shots.caption: Detail from The Last Day of Pompeii, Karl Bryullov
Vesuvius erupting in 1944, a much smaller eruption

scenes.narration: These currents swept through Herculaneum, on the coast closer to the volcano, and then through Pompeii. Anyone still in the town was killed. After that, Pompeii was silent. The whole eruption had lasted less than two days.

shots.file: File:Destruction of Pompeii and Herculaneum.jpg
shots.query: Destruction of Pompeii and Herculaneum John Martin
shots.caption: The Destruction of Pompeii and Herculaneum, John Martin, 1822

shots.file: File:Herculaneum, past, present and future (1908) (14596160389).jpg
shots.caption: Herculaneum, from a book published in 1908

scenes.narration: Afterwards, the towns lay buried under a thick layer of volcanic deposits. Over the centuries, even their locations were forgotten. In the late sixteenth century, workers digging a canal cut straight through buried walls and paintings without realising what they had found.

shots.file: File:Historical map of excavations in Pompeii.jpg
shots.caption: A historical map of the excavations at Pompeii
A Pompeian wall painting

scenes.narration: Systematic excavations began in 1748, under the Bourbon kings of Naples. Treasure hunters and scholars came first, then visitors from across Europe. Since then, around two thirds of the ancient town has been uncovered, street by street and house by house.

shots.file: File:Filippo Palizzi - Scavi a Pompei (1870).jpg
shots.caption: Excavations at Pompeii, painted by Filippo Palizzi, 1870

shots.file: File:Sommer, Giorgio - n. 2330 - ''Pompei - Anfiteatro'' - ca. 1869.jpg
shots.caption: Pompeii's amphitheatre, photographed around 1869

scenes.narration: In the 1860s, the archaeologist Giuseppe Fiorelli noticed hollow spaces in the hardened ash, left where bodies had decayed. He had them filled with plaster. The casts that emerged show people and animals in their final positions. They remain some of the most moving images from the ancient world.

shots.file: File:Giuseppe Fiorelli.jpg
shots.caption: Giuseppe Fiorelli, director of the Pompeii excavations

shots.file: File:Pompeii Plaster cast of a victim.jpg
shots.caption: A plaster cast of a victim of the eruption

scenes.narration: The remains of more than a thousand people have been found at Pompeii so far. Part of the town is still unexcavated, and many people probably fled, so the real death toll is unknown. Each cast is a reminder that these were individuals, not statistics.

shots.query: Pompeii Garden of the Fugitives casts
shots.caption: The Garden of the Fugitives, Pompeii
Casts displayed at Pompeii

scenes.narration: For centuries, the date seemed settled. Surviving copies of Pliny's letter give it as the twenty-fourth of August. But Pliny's original letter is lost. The copies were made by hand over many centuries, and they do not all agree.

shots.file: File:Pliny the Younger, Letters, Biblioteca Malatestiana.jpg
shots.caption: A manuscript of Pliny the Younger's letters

shots.file: File:Pliny the Younger.jpg
shots.caption: Pliny the Younger, as imagined by a later artist

scenes.narration: At Pompeii, archaeologists had long noticed things that did not fit a summer date, such as autumn fruits and heating braziers in homes. Then in 2018, a faint charcoal inscription was found on a wall in a house under renovation. It records a date equivalent to the seventeenth of October.

shots.caption: Pomegranates in a Roman wall painting
A house in Pompeii's Regio V excavations

scenes.narration: Why does a few weeks matter? The date shapes how we read the ruins. The food in the kitchens, the clothes people wore and the building work under way all tell a different story in autumn.

shots.caption: A still life of food, from a Pompeian wall painting
Carbonised bread found at Pompeii

scenes.narration: If that note was written in AD 79, the eruption came later, perhaps around the twenty-fourth of October, as Pompeii's archaeological park has proposed. Other scholars disagree. They argue the charcoal could have survived longer, or that the letter is still the best evidence. The debate is not settled.

shots.caption: Writing on a wall in Pompeii

shots.file: File:Timeline map of the excavations in Pompeii.png
shots.caption: Map showing when each part of Pompeii was excavated

scenes.narration: Whatever the exact day, Pompeii gives us something written history rarely does. Not only emperors and battles, but bakers, shopkeepers and families, caught in the middle of their lives. Their paintings, graffiti and kitchens show how ordinary Romans actually lived.

shots.file: File:Roman fresco Villa dei Misteri Pompeii 001.jpg
shots.caption: Fresco from the Villa of the Mysteries, Pompeii

shots.file: File:Villa of the Mysteries (Pompeii) - frescos 02.jpg
shots.caption: The painted walls of the Villa of the Mysteries

scenes.narration: And the work is far from finished. The 2018 inscription was itself a new find, turned up during recent work on the site. Every season, archaeologists uncover more rooms, more paintings and more traces of the people who lived there.

shots.caption: Recent excavations at Pompeii

shots.file: File:Roman fresco Villa dei Misteri Pompeii 005.jpg
shots.caption: Detail of the frescoes in the Villa of the Mysteries

scenes.narration: Vesuvius is still an active volcano, and millions of people live around the Bay of Naples today. The story of AD 79 is not only about the past. Sources and image credits are in the description.
